name: The Great Tsukubane-gashi of Uneyama Shrine

location.address: Uneyama Shrine, 787 Kiyotake, Toyosaka-cho, Higashi-Hiroshima, Hiroshima Prefecture

access: Shrine grounds, open 24 hours, no admission fee, no staff on site. Parking and a restroom are provided.

Uneyama Shrine, on a hilltop in Toyosaka-cho Kiyotake, was founded 1151 and moved to its current site in the Muromachi period. Its whole giant-tree grove, five species and eight individual trees, was designated a Hiroshima Prefecture Natural Monument (dive-hiroshima.com and the prefecture's own cultural-property listing both describe it). Independent sources single out an 'Oo-tsukubanegashi' as among the largest of its species in the prefecture, which matches this register entry both on species and on standing out from its neighbours. The grove suffered major damage in a 1991 typhoon and was restored by the shrine's parishioners. Location is the shrine's neighbourhood centroid (Nominatim could not resolve the shrine itself), so location_precision stays approximate; this is one of four register trees at the same site (hgh_023-026), all part of the same named grove.

name: The Asunaro of Renkyo-ji

location.address: Renkyo-ji, 2577 Kiyotake, Toyosaka-cho, Higashi-Hiroshima, Hiroshima Prefecture

access: Temple grounds in Toyosaka-cho Kiyotake, presumed open in daylight like the area's other temples; no gate or restriction found.

verify_notes: Report ID 53634, Ministry of Environment giant-tree register, surveyed 1988: girth 3.30m, health noted as partial dieback. Independently and specifically confirmed by the city's own cultural-properties page, higashihiroshima.lg.jp, which designated this exact tree a City Natural Monument on 1 March 1975 (Showa 50), gives the same girth, 3.3m, and a height of 17m, and records that a branch removed for safety in 1982 showed 170 growth rings, giving a real documented lower bound on the tree's age (basis: growth-ring count on a removed branch, not the whole trunk, so the trunk itself is at least this old and plausibly older). A 1981 prefectural giant-tree survey recorded it as the largest Asunaro (hiba) in Hiroshima Prefecture. The tree has been repeatedly struck by lightning, with damaged branches cut back each time, which is the source of both the dieback note and the ring count. This is one of the best-evidenced trees in this batch: exact species, exact girth agreement between two independent sources 38 years apart, a formal age floor from a real ring count, and an official designation. Address (2577 Kiyotake) could not be individually geocoded; used the Kiyotake neighbourhood centroid, so location_precision stays approximate despite the strong documentation otherwise.

name: The Chinaberry Trees of Kurose Central Park

location.address: Kurose Central Park, former Nakakurose Elementary School site, Maruyama, Kurose-cho, Higashi-Hiroshima, Hiroshima Prefecture

access: Free, public park (Kurose Central Park). Both trunks are fenced off to protect the roots; visitors may walk right up to the fence but not inside it.
transport: No train station in the immediate area; Kurose-cho is served by local buses from Saijo, and the park is reachable by car.
verify_notes: Report ID 53622, Ministry of Environment giant-tree register, surveyed 1988: girth 3.51m for a single entry, health good, age band 100-199 years. The city's own designation, made a City Natural Monument on 28 April 2022, is far more specific and describes TWO trees standing together in a 412.66 sqm protected area: a western trunk of 4.53m girth and 19.5m height, and an eastern trunk of 4.70m girth and 15.3m height. Both sources agree these are the largest Chinaberry trees recorded in Hiroshima Prefecture. The planting date is documented, not inferred: both trees were planted in 1912 (Meiji 45) at the schoolyard of the former Nakakurose Elementary School, which closed and was redeveloped as a public park (Kurose Central Park) around the trees rather than the trees being added to an existing park, so this is a genuine documented planting date for the specimens themselves, giving an age of roughly 114 years as of 2026 (age_min/age_max given a small band either side for month-of-planting uncertainty). The register's single 3.51m figure is noticeably smaller than either of the city's two later trunk measurements; flagged as a discrepancy for the writer, most likely explained by the register recording only one of the two trunks, or measuring lower or higher on the trunk, or simply 22+ years of growth between the 2000-era survey and the 2022 designation. Presented as one entry since the two trunks stand together in one small fenced plot and read as a single destination, per the register-twins convention.
